title: Hesperus Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hesperus wells have a 160 ft median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $14,000-$24,000.
h1: Hesperus, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Hesperus means evaluating more than a permit number. Records within 5 miles show how deep local wells tend to be, what reported yields look like, and what a new well may cost in this part of La Plata County.

Most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, so results can change substantially between nearby parcels. Use neighboring wells as a starting point, not a guarantee. A driller still needs to evaluate the lot, access, geology, casing and grout requirements, pump equipment, and the proposed household use.

sections.heading: Hesperus well depths reflect fractured bedrock and mixed ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Hesperus is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 102 to 360 feet, which is a wide spread for estimating a new-well bid. A well near the median might be straightforward, but a parcel toward the deeper end can require much more drilling, casing, and labor.

Depth records range as deep as 1,000 feet. About 21% of wells are under 100 feet, 48% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 28% are from 300 to 600 feet. The local drilling model describes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, while permits most often name fractured bedrock. That combination helps explain why neighboring properties can differ. Marvel, Durango, and Mancos provide useful comparison areas, but Hesperus records are the better guide for a Hesperus parcel.

sections.heading: Reported Hesperus yields are usually workable, but verify the well
sections.html:
Only 77 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are useful but not a guarantee for every property. Among those reports, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for a household well when the storage system and pump are properly sized.

Yield results are uneven. About 64% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 16% report more than 15, and 18% report 1 to 5. About 3% are under 1 gallon per minute. A low-yield well may still serve a home with adequate storage, but it deserves a different design and a careful conversation with the driller before closing.

sections.heading: Water levels near Hesperus need parcel-level checking
sections.html:
Only 20 permits report a static water level, so the water-level sample is small. Those records show a median depth to water of 64 feet, with the middle half from 50 to 299 feet. The spread is more important than the median for a buyer: water may be relatively shallow at one location and much deeper at another.

The available permit history does not provide enough water-level observations by decade to establish a reliable falling or rising trend. Do not treat the 64-foot median as a guaranteed pumping depth. Ask for the well construction report, static level, pumping information, and any recent service records for the specific property. A licensed driller can also explain how the expected water level affects pump placement, tank size, electrical work, and operating cost.

sections.heading: Hesperus permit activity shows long local drilling history
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show 736 permitted wells within the Hesperus search area. Of those, 468 are recorded as constructed, 501 report a total depth, and 77 report a pump yield. The record is therefore broad, but not every permit gives the same level of useful information.

Permitting began with 1 record in the 1950s and 2 in the 1960s. Activity increased to 79 in the 1970s, 96 in the 1980s, 180 in the 1990s, and 173 in the 2000s. There are 52 permits in the 2010s and 18 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Beeman Bros Drilling Inc. accounts for 78 records under J. L. Beeman and 64 under Matthew N. Beeman. Dak Drilling LLC, associated with Doug Rathjen, appears on 53.

sections.heading: A new Hesperus well commonly starts with a five-figure budget
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, drilling is estimated at $50 to $75 per foot. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,000 to $12,000. That figure is not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $14,000 to $24,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, unusual casing or grout needs, and site-specific electrical or trenching conditions can move the final bid outside that range. When comparing lots near Hesperus, Marvel, or the Durango side of the area, ask for a written estimate that separates drilling from completion and identifies what happens if the hole produces little water.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole risk before closing
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 11 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped information. These facts do not determine water quality at a particular well, but they are reasons to review nearby land uses and test the water after purchase or before relying on a new well.

Most local permits are for domestic or household use at 90%; stock use is 12%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 4%. Confirm that the permit allows the intended use, especially if the plan includes livestock, irrigation, or additional structures. Check septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway access, and building placement before drilling. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. A low-yield or dry hole is a real construction risk, particularly where fractured bedrock changes over short distances.

sections.heading: Use nearby permits to price a Hesperus lot before building
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the closest DWR well permits and compare depth, reported yield, static water level, completion details, and use. A group of nearby wells with similar depths is more useful than the overall Hesperus median. Pay particular attention to wells reporting less than 1 gallon per minute, because they show that limited production is present in the broader record even though the median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute.

For a buildable lot, confirm legal access for a drilling rig, space for the well and septic system, electrical routing, and room for a replacement septic area. Have a Colorado-licensed driller review the parcel before relying on a seller's estimate. If the property already has a well, request the permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and service history. Those documents can be more valuable than a countywide average.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hesperus, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Hesperus is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 102 to 360 feet. About 48% of wells are 100 to 300 feet, while 28% are 300 to 600 feet. Records reach 1,000 feet, so a local driller should review nearby permits before pricing a parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Hesperus?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,000 to $12,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,000 to $24,000. Access, depth, casing, grout, and difficult ground can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Hesperus wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 77 Hesperus-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 10.0. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 64% report 5 to 15. These figures are not a guarantee; fractured-bedrock production can vary between neighboring lots.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Hesperus, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield alone. The mapped area includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 11 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well and review nearby land uses. For a new well, plan water-quality testing after construction.

faq.q: Do Hesperus wells need an augmentation plan?
faq.a: The permit records show 90% domestic or household use, 12% stock, 1% irrigation, and 4% monitoring. Whether an augmentation plan is required depends on the water right, basin status, permit terms, and proposed use. In an over-appropriated basin, confirm the requirements with Colorado DWR or a water attorney before adding irrigation, livestock use, or other demands.
